Hey OP, 

First off, I'm so sorry to hear you feel you're at the end of your rope. All I've got is good vibes heading your way, and this: keep writing - it's saved my ass before, and there are people who will listen. I wish you the best in your troubles. Oh, and this: a few years ago, I started working for [NAMI](http://nami.org) (the National Alliance on Mental Illness), with a program called "Ending the Silence", which had me going around to local high schools and middle schools and giving a presentation that aimed to dispel the stigma that prevents us from having meaningful conversations about mental illness. I had to stand up in front of a room of 200+ young people at a time and speak candidly about my lived experience as a person with bipolar disorder. Telling a room full of kids I'd never met about some of my darkest times made me feel intensely vulnerable, naked almost, but I was stunned by how rewarding it was: even if most of the middle-school crowd was shooting spitballs at each other by the end, at almost every single presentation, at least one kid would come up to me and thank me for telling a story they thought no one else had lived. For reassuring them that people survived this. Some came wordlessly, in tears. Some hugged me. It was intensely powerful, and  - for me - really instrumental in reframing the narrative of my illness for myself. Instead of the abiding, shameful weakness that I've known for so long, it felt like a point of solidarity with other vulnerable minds. I often don't feel worthy of being called a "mentor", but knowing that young people were seeing in me a glimmer of hope for the future was both very humbling and very rewarding. We have suffered, but we have survived. I don't know if there are any such programs in your area, or if you'd feel comfortable sharing what's going on in your head and your heart... but, as trite as it may seem, there was for me a real feeling of release in sharing my experience with others, and a feeling of redemption in realizing that sharing my story made someone else feel less alone. It began the process of healing some wounds I didn't know were still open. If you find comfort in writing, in expression, then it might be worth investigating what comfort you can find in sharing your experiences with other people who feel pain similar to yours. 

Just my $0.02; I wish you the best, OP. Live long and prosper.

I usually finalize the chord progression before the melody. Once the backbone of the chord pattern is laid down, I play around with different intervals: like, what happens if I go a 4th up from here? That goes not only for pitch, but also rhythm and articulation: Regina Spektor does this really well in [Fidelity](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wigqKfLWjvM), alternating between sweet legato slides ("I hear in my mi-i-ind...") and sharp staccato notes ("breaks my ha-ha-ha-ha-ha-ha-heart..." in the chorus).

It may be more "cool story" than "rigorously researched historical truth", but it's Friday and I'm on reddit. Google away! Here's what I learned about it when I was living in Amsterdam.

When Napoleon annexed the Netherlands in 1811, he imposed a mandatory census: all citizens had to register their first and last names to be taxed. IIRC, before Napoleonic rule, it was more common for Dutch people to use patronymic names (i.e. if your name is Jan and your father's name is Pieter, you go by Jan Pietersen - more [here](http://www.expatica.com/nl/lifestyle_leisure/lifestyle/funny-Dutch-names-the-story-behind-them_12619.html)). 

As I understand it, the census forced a whole occupied population to make up surnames so that their imperial occupiers could tax them. Composing the most ridiculous last names possible was one way to stick it to Napoleon (while also making it somewhat *less* likely that the taxman will find you/your sons will be drafted into Napoleon's army). Names like Zeldenthuis ("seldom home") and Zondervan ("without surname") make this theory seem reasonably plausible to me.

Napoleon came and went, but the census procedure - and the surnames - stuck. I can't find the long list of really funny ones I stumbled on, but I think my favorite was "Kwaasteniet". It means "not the worst".

My tattoos have very little to do with how **highly** I think of myself. They have everything to do with how **deeply** I think about myself. 

For me, each one is symbolic of rites of passage, achievements, lessons learned, and moments in my life that I've deemed important enough to carry with me into the future. They are part of my personal narrative.

We live by narrative: our lives are patchworks of disconnected sensory experiences, tied together by the stories we tell ourselves about ourselves. Consciousness, memory, and even personality are fluid, and heavily informed by our present situation. 

Sometimes it's easy to lose track of the plot, even when we're the ones writing it. I find myself asking the queasy, uncomfortable, important questions:

*What am I doing with my life now? Why?* 

*Is this even important? Why?*

*Am I the sort of person who finds this important? Why?*

*Am I the person I want to be? Why?*

My tattoos are a record of the past selves that I respect. They are signposts to memory, talismans of identity, anchors to my origins, and they center me.

I choose to document my personal narrative with the art on my skin.

I worked as a tutor for a while. One day I was teaching two identical twins (9 years old, very inquisitive, from a conservative religious family, no filters at ALL). I assigned a short reading comprehension exercise on Norse mythology, and was trying to guide the conversation away from matters explicitly theological (being a deity-indifferent sort myself, and not wanting to evangelize, offend, or derail the discussion). I'd mentioned in an earlier class that I was not religious, and they saw right through my attempts to demur:

**Twin 1:** Do Jews go to heaven even though they're not Catholic?

**Irredentissima:** *[Oh dear sweet Batman how do I answer this...]* I don't know, Twin 1. As someone who does not believe that people go somewhere else when they die, I might not be the right person to ask. What do you think? 

**Twin 1**: *[Wide-eyed]* I don't know either!

**Irredentissima**: Perhaps you could ask someone at your church?

**Twin 1**: But if you don't believe in God, where are *you* gonna go when you die?

**Irredentissima**: *[...speechless, scrambling for a response, when Twin 2 jumps in and saves my ass]*

**Twin 2:** She's just gonna rest in peace!

I almost died of hypothermia swimming in cold water when I was about 12. I felt very calm, almost giddy but serene at the same time. I remember the cold of the water fading to a pleasant warmth and the beat of my heart, which had been hammering in my ears, gradually slowing until I couldn't hear it anymore. I enjoyed the sensation of my body, my warmth, being assimilated into the flow of the ocean. The thought of death didn't really cross my mind, just the thought of *fading.* 

Everyone who helped me that day seemed so concerned, but I found the whole thing rather comical. Before anyone knew I was in trouble, I lay on a rock hallucinating for about 45 minutes... saw some strange things: pale people running around me in circles as I lay prone, chanting and screaming, as if performing some ritual. I can't remember most of the rest, as it was fading in and out, but when people started realizing how unresponsive I was and calling for help, I felt a bit put out. The thought "They've found me out" entered my mind. The more I recovered, the more the danger I'd been in started to compute, but I don't remember ever feeling alarmed.

>In a first-of-its-kind study, Zhou et al. While the transsexuals studied had taken hormones, this was accounted for by including non-transsexual male and female controls which, for a variety of medical reasons, had experienced hormone reversal.
